analysis.one_liner: Requires voter-verified paper ballots for federal elections and funds states to replace hackable voting machines.
analysis.headline: The Election Security Act, with 40 cosponsors, never left the Senate committee it was referred to and died without a vote before the 2020 election.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require every state to use voter-verified paper ballots in federal elections, make paper the official record for recounts, and pay states at least $1 billion to replace voting machines that don't meet the standard. It would fund risk-limiting audits that catch wrong results, let independent experts probe election systems for holes through a bug bounty program, require voting machines to be made in the United States, and require federal agencies to share election threat information with state officials. It was referred to the Senate Rules and Administration Committee on the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, a markup, or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Voters, who would get a paper record of every vote that can be hand-counted in recounts and audits; state and local election officials, who would receive federal grants (at least $1 per average ballots cast, plus $175 million per year in later years) to replace noncompliant machines and harden their systems; voters with disabilities, non-English speakers, and voters with low literacy, who would benefit from funded research on accessible paper-ballot verification; and US voting machine manufacturers, which would gain a large federal market under the made-in-America requirement.

how_it_helps.text: Requires every voting system in federal elections to use an individual, durable, voter-verified paper ballot that the voter can inspect before casting, and makes the paper ballot the official record in recounts and audits [S2] [S3].

Authorizes $1 billion for fiscal 2019 plus $175 million in each of fiscal 2020, 2022, 2024, and 2026 in grants so states can replace noncompliant systems, run security improvements, and adopt better ballot design, with at least $1 per average ballots cast per state [S3].
Authorizes $20 million in grants for states to conduct risk-limiting audits, post-election checks with a known statistical chance of catching and correcting a wrong outcome [S2] [S3].

Requires the Department of Homeland Security to share timely threat information with chief state election officials, help expedite security clearances for them, and conduct vulnerability assessments on request, and requires a pre-election threat assessment from the Director of National Intelligence before each federal election [S2] [S3].
Creates an Election Security Bug Bounty Program paying independent experts to find and report vulnerabilities in election systems, participation by officials and vendors to be voluntary [S2] [S3].

Requires voting systems and paper ballots to be manufactured in the United States, with ballots printed on recycled US-made paper starting in 2021, and restricts grant funds to vendors owned by US citizens or permanent residents that disclose foreign sourcing and report cybersecurity incidents within 3 days [S2] [S3].

Requires the Election Assistance Commission to test voting hardware and software against current guidelines before each federal election and decertify systems that fail, and brings electronic poll books under voting-system rules [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers fund the grants (roughly $1.7 billion authorized over the period, plus research and audit grants); states absorb the work of replacing equipment and running audits; and voting machine vendors bear compliance costs from testing, decertification, incident-reporting, and US-manufacturing requirements.

drawbacks.text: The bill imposes uniform federal equipment and counting mandates on elections that states and counties have traditionally run, and jurisdictions using paper-record printers in 2018 would have had to keep offering hand-marked paper ballots at every polling place until 2022, adding cost and complexity on a tight timeline [S3].

Recounts and audits of federal elections would have to be counted by hand from paper, which election officials warn is slower and more expensive than machine counting, even though it is the audit standard security experts prefer [S3].

Paper ballots and audits address falsified or manipulated vote counts but do not by themselves address the other threats the bill itself names: disinformation campaigns and influence operations, which the bill handles mainly through studies, a national strategy, and a commission rather than enforceable rules [S2] [S3].
Buy-American and qualified-vendor requirements could shrink the pool of eligible suppliers and raise equipment prices for the states paying the difference [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is federal money and a one-time equipment replacement burden in exchange for a durable guarantee that every federal vote exists on a voter-verifiable paper record that can be recounted by hand, plus statistical audits and federal threat-sharing. Security researchers broadly consider paper ballots with risk-limiting audits the strongest practical defense against manipulated electronic tallies, and the bill's cost is modest next to what states were already spending on replacements. The weaker parts are the response to disinformation, which is largely advisory, and the tight federal deadlines on locally run elections.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the Senate Rules and Administration Committee the day it was introduced and sat there without a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote until that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Klobuchar introduced the bill on May 16, 2019, joined by 40 cosponsors including the Democratic leader and independents Bernie Sanders and Angus King [S1] [S4] [S5].
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Rules and Administration; no further action of any kind appears in the record [S5].
The bill never received a hearing, committee vote, or floor vote, and the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021, killing it [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Incumbent election-technology vendors kept selling paperless and noncompliant systems with no new testing, decertification, or US-manufacturing requirements, and states kept bearing the full cost of modernizing without federal grant help going into the 2020 election. Senate leadership also avoided pre-election votes on election security measures.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Election technology vendors and Senate leadership

sides.party_line_note: All 40 cosponsors were Democrats or independents; no Republican signed on, and the Republican-run committee and Senate majority never acted on it.

industries.note: The bill routes federal grant money to states to buy compliant systems, making private vendors the permanent channel for election infrastructure while imposing new rules on them: US ownership, foreign-sourcing disclosure, 3-day incident reporting, and independent testing with decertification. Vendors gain a large guaranteed market but lose the freedom to sell paperless or loosely monitored systems.

Vendors whose business rests on direct-recording electronic machines without voter-verifiable paper trails would lose that market entirely, since every federal vote must have a voter-verified paper ballot. Their interests run against the public's here because the product being priced out is the one that cannot be recounted or audited.
Ballots for federal elections would have to be printed in the United States on recycled US-made paper starting in 2021, creating a mandated domestic market.
